questions.stem: A client is prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin for angina. Which statement indicates correct understanding?
questions.tip: SL nitro: sit down, 1 tab every 5 min x3, call 911 if unrelieved.

opts.t: “I’ll sit down before I place the tablet under my tongue.”
opts.r: Correct. Nitroglycerin causes vasodilation and can drop blood pressure, so sitting prevents falls from dizziness.

opts.t: “I’ll swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.”
opts.r: Sublingual tablets dissolve under the tongue; swallowing bypasses the intended absorption.

opts.t: “If my chest pain continues, I’ll wait 30 minutes before taking another.”
opts.r: The interval is every 5 minutes up to 3 doses — 30 minutes delays needed care.

opts.t: “I’ll keep the tablets in a clear plastic pill organizer.”
opts.r: Nitroglycerin degrades in light; it must stay in its original dark glass bottle.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning fall-prevention measures for a high-risk older adult. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Keep the bed in the lowest position
opts.r: Correct. A low bed reduces injury if the client attempts to get up.

opts.t: Ensure the call light is within reach
opts.r: Correct. Easy access lets the client summon help instead of getting up alone.

opts.t: Raise all four side rails
opts.r: Incorrect. Four raised rails are a restraint and can worsen injury if the client climbs over.

opts.t: Provide non-skid footwear
opts.r: Correct. Non-skid soles reduce slipping.

opts.t: Keep the room dimly lit at all times
opts.r: Incorrect. Poor lighting increases fall risk; provide adequate lighting.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client 6 hours after abdominal surgery. Select the 3 findings that require immediate follow-up.

opts.t: Oxygen saturation 88% on room air
opts.r: Correct. Hypoxemia needs prompt intervention (positioning, oxygen).

opts.t: Urine output 15 mL over the last 2 hours
opts.r: Correct. Oliguria (<30 mL/hr) may signal hypovolemia or shock.

opts.t: Rigid, distended abdomen with rebound tenderness
opts.r: Correct. Signs of possible internal bleeding or peritonitis.

opts.t: Pain rated 4/10 relieved by repositioning
opts.r: Incorrect. Mild, relieved pain is expected post-op.

opts.t: Serosanguineous drainage lightly staining the dressing
opts.r: Incorrect. A small amount of serosanguineous drainage is expected early.

questions.stem: Sort each newborn finding as Expected or Requires follow-up.

opts.t: Acrocyanosis of the hands and feet
opts.r: Expected. Bluish extremities are normal in the early newborn period.

opts.t: Central cyanosis of the lips and trunk
opts.r: Requires follow-up. Central cyanosis indicates inadequate oxygenation.

opts.t: Heart rate 140 beats/min
opts.r: Expected. Normal newborn range is 110–160.

opts.t: A single palmar crease with low-set ears
opts.r: Requires follow-up. May indicate a chromosomal condition needing evaluation.

questions.stem: Order: heparin infusion 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W at 800 units/hour. At how many mL/hour should the nurse set the pump? Record to the nearest whole number.
questions.r: 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. 800 units/hr ÷ 100 units/mL = 8 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Place the steps for donning personal protective equipment (PPE) in the correct order.

items.r: Hand hygiene comes first, before any PPE.
The gown is donned first among the garments.

items.t: Put on the mask or respirator
Put on goggles or face shield

items.r: Gloves go on last, pulled over the gown cuffs.

questions.stem: A nurse will auscultate the apical pulse (point of maximal impulse). Identify the correct location on the chest diagram.
questions.media: Anterior chest diagram with labeled regions: (a) 2nd intercostal space right sternal border, (b) 2nd intercostal space left sternal border, (c) left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line, (d) right lower costal margin.

regions.label: 2nd ICS, right sternal border
regions.r: This is the aortic area, not the PMI.

regions.label: Left 5th ICS, midclavicular line
regions.r: Correct. The apical pulse/PMI is auscultated here (mitral area).

regions.label: Right lower costal margin
regions.r: This overlies the liver, not the apex of the heart.

questions.stem: Review the client's record. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene first?
questions.media: Tabbed EHR: Vitals, Labs, Orders, Nurses' Notes.

tabs.orders: IV normal saline bolus, blood cultures x2, broad-spectrum antibiotics
tabs.notes: Client confused, skin warm and flushed, urine output 15 mL last hour

opts.t: Hypotension with tachycardia and elevated lactate
opts.r: Correct. These signal septic shock — the priority requiring immediate fluid resuscitation.

opts.t: Temperature of 38.9°C
opts.r: Fever is expected in infection but is not the most urgent finding here.

opts.t: White blood cell count of 18,000
opts.r: Leukocytosis supports infection but is not the immediate life threat.

opts.t: Warm, flushed skin
opts.r: A finding of early/warm shock, but the hemodynamic instability is the priority.

questions.stem: The monitor shows the rhythm below. Which rhythm strip matches a client in ventricular fibrillation?
questions.media: Four described ECG strips shown as answer options.

opts.t: A chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable P waves, QRS, or T waves
opts.r: Correct. V-fib is disorganized electrical activity with no discernible complexes — a shockable emergency.

opts.t: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at 80 bpm with a P wave before each QRS
opts.r: This is normal sinus rhythm.

opts.t: A sawtooth baseline with regular atrial waves at ~300/min
opts.r: This describes atrial flutter.

opts.t: A completely flat line
opts.r: This is asystole, not V-fib.

questions.stem: Listen to the recorded breath sounds auscultated at the bases. Which finding is most consistent with what is heard?
questions.media: Audio clip: fine, high-pitched crackling sounds heard on inspiration at the lung bases.

opts.t: Fine crackles suggesting fluid in the alveoli
opts.r: Correct. Fine inspiratory crackles at the bases suggest fluid, as in heart failure or pneumonia.

opts.t: Expiratory wheezes from bronchoconstriction
opts.r: Wheezes are musical and expiratory, not crackling.

opts.t: A pleural friction rub
opts.r: A rub is a grating sound, not fine crackles.

opts.t: Normal vesicular breath sounds
opts.r: Crackles are adventitious — not normal breath sounds.

questions.stem: Review the client's 8-hour intake and output below. What is the nurse's best interpretation?

opts.t: The client has a net positive fluid balance and reduced urine output
opts.r: Correct. Intake 1200 vs output 400 = +800 mL, and urine 250 mL/8 hr is low — monitor for retention/overload.

opts.t: The client is dehydrated and needs fluid restriction
opts.r: Intake exceeds output; fluid restriction would be inappropriate reasoning here.

opts.t: Intake and output are balanced
opts.r: They are not — intake far exceeds output.

opts.t: Urine output is within expected limits
opts.r: 250 mL over 8 hr (~31 mL/hr) is at the low end and warrants monitoring.

questions.stem: A client receiving an IV antibiotic suddenly develops hives, lip swelling, wheezing, and BP 82/40. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition, the actions to take, and the parameters to monitor.

options.r: Correct. Acute onset of hives, airway swelling, wheezing, and hypotension after a drug is anaphylaxis.
A panic attack does not cause hives, lip swelling, or hypotension.
Overload causes crackles and hypertension, not hives and hypotension.
Correct. Removing the trigger is essential.
Correct. Epinephrine is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis.

options.t: Administer the next scheduled dose of the antibiotic
options.r: Incorrect and dangerous — continuing the trigger worsens the reaction.

options.t: Place the client in a high-Fowler’s position and restrict fluids
options.r: Incorrect. The client needs fluids for hypotension, not restriction.
Correct. Airway swelling can progress to obstruction.
Correct. Monitor for worsening or resolving distributive shock.
Not the acute monitoring priority in anaphylaxis.
Not the acute priority here.

questions.stem: The client's vital signs are trended below over 6 hours. What is the nurse's best interpretation of the trend?

opts.t: The client is deteriorating toward shock and needs urgent intervention
opts.r: Correct. Rising HR/RR with falling BP and SpO2 is a classic worsening-shock trend.

opts.t: The client is stable and improving
opts.r: The trend is clearly worsening, not improving.

opts.t: The changes are expected and need no action
opts.r: A progressive decline in perfusion always warrants action.

opts.t: The client is over-sedated
opts.r: Sedation would lower HR/RR, not raise them.

questions.stem: For each assessment finding, indicate whether it suggests fluid volume DEFICIT or fluid volume EXCESS.

rows.t: Bounding pulse and distended neck veins
rows.r: Bounding pulse and JVD reflect fluid overload.

rows.t: Dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor
rows.r: Dry mucosa and tenting indicate deficit.
Low BP with compensatory tachycardia points to deficit.

questions.stem: For each medication, select ALL routes by which it can be safely administered.

rows.r: Regular insulin is the only insulin given IV, and is also given subcutaneously — never PO (destroyed by digestion).
Heparin is given IV or subcutaneously, not orally.

questions.stem: For each laboratory value, select whether it is LOW, WITHIN NORMAL LIMITS, or HIGH.

options.r: Correct. Normal potassium is 3.5–5.0 mEq/L; 2.9 is low.
2.9 is below the normal range.
2.9 is low, not high.
140 is normal.
Correct. Normal sodium is 135–145 mEq/L.
140 is normal.
320 is elevated, not low.
Fasting normal is ~70–110 mg/dL.
Correct. 320 mg/dL is hyperglycemic.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting the correct options.
questions.sentence: For a conscious client with a blood glucose of 52 mg/dL, the nurse should first {{0}} and then {{1}}.

options.t: give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.r: Correct. The Rule of 15: treat with 15 g fast carbs.
Incorrect — insulin lowers glucose further.
Incorrect — the client needs carbohydrate.

options.t: recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes
options.r: Correct. Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still low.
Too long — recheck at 15 minutes.
Not the immediate next step.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence to explain the nurse's clinical reasoning.
questions.sentence: The client is most likely experiencing {{0}} as evidenced by {{1}}.

options.r: Correct. Nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green vision with a low potassium point to digoxin toxicity.
MI presents with chest pain and ECG changes, not yellow-green vision.
Hypoglycemia causes shakiness and diaphoresis, not visual halos.

options.t: nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green visual halos with a potassium of 3.1
options.r: Correct. These are classic toxicity signs; hypokalemia increases the risk.

options.t: a fever of 38.9°C and productive cough
options.r: These suggest infection, not digoxin toxicity.
Hypertension alone does not indicate digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings in the nurse's note that require immediate follow-up.

segments.t: Reports new shortness of breath and chest tightness.
segments.r: Requires follow-up — possible cardiac or pulmonary emergency.

segments.t: Left calf swollen, red, and tender to touch.

questions.stem: Highlight each vital sign value that is outside normal limits for an adult.
A 68-year-old client with a history of heart failure presents to the clinic. Use the record to answer the six questions.
questions.scenario: A 68-year-old client with chronic heart failure reports 3 days of worsening shortness of breath, trouble sleeping flat, and swelling in both legs.

tabs.history: Chronic heart failure, hypertension, type 2 diabetes.
tabs.vitals: BP 158/94, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 90% on room air, weight up 4 kg in 3 days.
tabs.orders: IV furosemide, daily weights, 2 g sodium diet, oxygen to keep SpO2 >94%.
tabs.nurses_notes: Bilateral crackles to mid-lung fields; 2+ pitting edema to the knees; jugular venous distention noted.

questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with worsening heart failure? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Bilateral crackles and SpO2 90%
opts.r: Correct. Pulmonary congestion and hypoxemia reflect fluid backing into the lungs.

opts.t: 4 kg weight gain in 3 days
opts.r: Correct. Rapid weight gain signals fluid retention.

opts.t: 2+ pitting edema and jugular venous distention
opts.r: Correct. Signs of fluid overload.

opts.t: Blood pressure 158/94
opts.r: Correct. Elevated afterload is consistent with decompensation.

opts.t: Potassium 3.4 mEq/L
opts.r: Incorrect for this item — hypokalemia is a lab concern (diuretic-related) but not a direct sign of worsening congestion.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it reflects FLUID OVERLOAD or a MEDICATION side effect to monitor.

rows.r: Hypokalemia is a furosemide side effect to monitor.
Over-diuresis/ACE inhibitor can affect renal function — a medication concern.

questions.stem: Which problem should the nurse prioritize?

opts.t: Impaired gas exchange related to pulmonary congestion
opts.r: Correct. Airway/breathing and oxygenation take priority (SpO2 90% with crackles).

opts.t: Risk for impaired skin integrity related to edema
opts.r: A valid concern but not the immediate priority over oxygenation.

opts.t: Deficient knowledge related to diet
opts.r: Important for teaching later, not the acute priority.

opts.t: Fatigue related to poor sleep
opts.r: Lowest priority compared with gas exchange.

questions.stem: Select the 3 most appropriate interventions to include in the plan of care.

opts.t: Administer IV furosemide as prescribed
opts.r: Correct. Diuresis reduces fluid overload.

opts.t: Apply oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 94%
opts.r: Correct. Corrects hypoxemia.

opts.t: Position the client in high-Fowler’s
opts.r: Correct. Upright positioning eases breathing and reduces preload.

opts.t: Encourage increased oral fluids
opts.r: Incorrect — the client is fluid overloaded.

opts.t: Provide a high-sodium diet
opts.r: Incorrect — sodium is restricted in heart failure.

questions.stem: Complete the nurse's next action.
questions.sentence: Because the client is receiving furosemide with a potassium of 3.4, the nurse should {{0}} and {{1}}.

options.r: Correct. Furosemide wastes potassium; hypokalemia risks dysrhythmias.
Incorrect — the client is already low.
Incorrect — not indicated.
Correct. Low potassium is typically replaced.
Incorrect — would worsen hypokalemia.
Incorrect — weights track fluid status.

questions.stem: After treatment, which finding best indicates the interventions were effective?

opts.t: SpO2 96%, clear lung sounds, and 2 kg weight loss
opts.r: Correct. Improved oxygenation, clearing congestion, and fluid loss show effective treatment.

opts.t: Weight increased by another 1 kg
opts.r: Weight gain indicates worsening fluid retention.

opts.t: Crackles now heard throughout all lung fields
opts.r: Worsening crackles show the congestion is not resolving.

opts.t: Urine output of 10 mL over 4 hours
opts.r: Very low output suggests diuresis is not working or worsening renal perfusion.
